newsitem.title: INDIA: Scandal paralyses government in Indian state.
newsitem.headline: Scandal paralyses government in Indian state.

text.p: The government of India's poverty-stricken state of Bihar has been paralysed by a $280 million farm funds scandal and its continuing fallout, politicians and businessmen said on Friday.

"There is total paralysis at least for the last 17 months, ever since the fodder case went to the high court," said Sushil Kumar Modi, the chief of the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in the state legislative assembly.

The so-called "fodder" scandal, which involves the alleged embezzlement of animal welfare funds, came to a head last Friday when Bihar state chief minister Laloo Prasad Yadav, a charismatic low-caste leader, resigned and named his wife as successor.
Yadav surrendered to a court on Wednesday after his attempts to win "anticipatory bail", following indictment by the federal police, failed.
He has been ordered held in judicial custody for two weeks while investigators question him in connection with the farm funds scandal.
Yadav says he is innocent. His critics say he has shirked work and misused civil servants while trying to prove his innocence.
Yadav's Rashtriya Janata Party (RJD) party called a state-wide general strike on Friday to press for its leader's release.
"Everything is ready (in official papers) in some cases but political decisions are not being taken," said an official of the Bihar Industries Association, who asked not to be identified.

He referred to a cold-rolled steel project by India's Tata group and said the project's approval was being delayed because the scandal had made officials shy of taking decisions that might attract scrutiny or accusation by the political opposition.
"Officers are not interested in working. Even otherwise, Bihar is not famous for its work," Modi said.
Backward Bihar, rich in minerals but prone to floods, caste politics and poverty, is often considered a problem state by federal administrators.

In Patna, government workers, thousands of whom are considered redundant, chewed tobacco or gossiped in the state secretariat building. Many officials were out for long lunches. Government buildings wore a deserted look on Friday.

Ganesh Prasad Yadav, leader of the Janata Dal from which Laloo Yadav broke away on July 5, said no significant decision on food, clothing, shelter, healthcare or law and order had been taken since April, when federal police indicted Laloo Yadav.
"I am not exaggerating," the politician said. "Travel on a flooded road here and your mind will open up."
Modi said one-fifth of Patna's one million citizens were affected by the flooding of roads earlier this month, when cars could not move and pedestrians had to wade through knee-deep water.
Some frustrated citizens petitioned the local high court, which described the administration as "jungle law."
Power cuts are frequent in Bihar, roads are uneven or unmade, and potholes are common in the state capital.
Modi said two of Laloo Yadav's own populist schemes had fallen into a black hole because of his political preoccupations.
One is a 400 million rupee ($11.2 million) plan to give cotton saris to poor women at 15 rupees a piece and the other is to give rice to the poor at two rupees a kg, Modi said.
Opposition leaders accused Laloo Yadav of favouritism in the civil service and politicising the administration.
"He has kept his own people in key posts," Modi said.
